children.text: A lakeside town on a highland at about

in South Cotabato, the homeland of the T'boli people. From the mist over the lake at dawn and its water lilies, to T'nalak cloth woven from patterns seen in dreams, to a zipline over Seven Falls, it brings together nature and indigenous culture in one place.

Lake Sebu is both a highland town in South Cotabato, in southern Mindanao, and the name of the lake surrounding it. Several lakes — Sebu, Seloton, Lahit, and others — sit together in a mountain basin at about

elevation, with the largest, Lake Sebu, covering about 350 hectares. Though it's in the tropics, the highland setting keeps mornings and evenings cool, and the lake is famous for the mist that rises over the water at sunrise. Don't confuse it with Cebu in the Visayas — despite the similar name, it's an entirely different place.

This is the homeland of the T'boli people, an indigenous group in the southern Philippines. The T'boli are known for T'nalak, a cloth woven from traditionally dyed abaca (Manila hemp) fiber, said to be woven from patterns the weaver has seen in a dream. The intricate designs, made only in red, black, and white, embody the community's worldview, earning it the nickname "the dream cloth." The T'nalak master weaver Lang Dulay was named a National Living Treasure (GAMABA) by the Philippine government, bringing this tradition to the world's attention.

The lake has long been central to T'boli life, and today it's dotted with tilapia fish farms, making fresh tilapia dishes a signature food of the region. In the forest south of the lake lies Seven Falls, a series of seven waterfalls arranged like steps, and the zipline crossing above them is known as one of the highest in the Philippines.

Lake Sebu is less a flashy resort than a place to experience indigenous culture close to nature. It suits anyone who enjoys slow travel — staying at a quiet lakeside lodge, watching the morning mist and water lilies, visiting a weaving workshop to talk with the artisans. It's a good fit for photographers, families who enjoy cultural experiences, and travelers touring southern Mindanao.
Ride a zipline split into two segments over the forest and waterfalls. The first segment runs over
with a considerable drop to the valley floor, giving an exhilarating view of the falls spread out below.

From the zipline's landing point, follow the steps and forest path down to see several falls up close, including the biggest and most dramatic, the second falls (Hikong Bente). With time and energy, you can trek even further down to the lower falls.

blocks.title: Dawn boat tour on the lake

children.text: A small boat tour at sunrise lets you see the mist, water lilies, tilapia farms, and residents rowing dugout canoes. It's the most beautiful hour at Lake Sebu.

At workshops like the Lang Dulay Weaving Center, you can watch abaca fiber tied, dyed, and woven on a loom. Since finishing a single bolt of cloth can take months, buying a piece is a meaningful way to support the artisans.

blocks.title: T'boli Museum and the School of Living Traditions

children.text: A small museum in a traditional house and the "School of Living Traditions" let you see T'boli instrument playing, traditional dance, and brass ornament craft. With advance notice, some places will put on a short performance.

Lakeside restaurants prepare tilapia in many ways — fried, grilled, or simmered in coconut milk, as well as tilapia sinigang and kinilaw. Eating lunch while looking out over the lake is one of the pleasures of a Lake Sebu trip.
A hillside viewpoint near the town offers a view of several overlapping lakes and mountains. The lake turning golden at dusk is a striking sight.

items.title: Chartered vehicle / getting around the village

children.text: If there are several of you, chartering a van for the day from General Santos (about
) is convenient and safer. Within Lake Sebu, habal-habal (motorbike taxi) is the main way to get around, costing about
one-way to Seven Falls or a weaving workshop. Lake boats are rented by the boat at your accommodation or a landing.

Being on a highland, Lake Sebu stays around 18–28 degrees year-round, cooler than the lowlands, and dawns can be cool enough to need long sleeves. Typhoon impact is minimal, but rain falls year-round; the comparatively drier
December
to
May
is best for trekking and boat tours. From
June
to
October
, afternoon showers are frequent, making the waterfall trails slippery, so it's best to concentrate your schedule in the morning.
Mist forms especially well on dry-season mornings, when the temperature swing is greatest. Every
November

, the Helobung Festival, Lake Sebu's signature event, brings traditional dance and music, costume processions, and craft exhibits from the T'boli, Ubo, and other indigenous groups. South Cotabato's province-wide T'nalak Festival is held every
July
in Koronadal. Accommodation can run short during these festivals, so book ahead.

Most accommodation lines the shore of Lake Sebu — lodges and resorts, many with bungalows extending over the water and restaurants with lake views, at about

a night. The long-running Punta Isla Lake Resort is well known for its lake views and tilapia dishes. Facilities are mostly simple, so expect weak hot water or slow Wi-Fi. For wider options, staying at a hotel in downtown Koronadal (about
1 hour 30 minutes
away) and visiting for the day is another choice.

Tilapia is clearly the star of the local food. You can try it fried crisp, charcoal-grilled, simmered in coconut milk (ginataan), in tangy sinigang, or cured in vinegar (kinilaw) — a single fish prepared many different ways. Lotus-root and vegetable dishes grown by the lakeside also pair well. On your way back to General Santos, don't skip the fresh tuna sashimi and grilled tuna jaw the city is famous for as "the tuna capital of the Philippines."
Lake Sebu has almost no reliable ATMs. Withdraw all the cash you'll need in General Santos or Koronadal.
The zipline has shorter lines and better weather in the morning. Since it stops running in the rain, it's safer to ride it first thing on day one.
The Seven Falls trekking section has many steps and slopes. Wear non-slip shoes, and bring trekking poles if your knees are weak.
Book the dawn boat tour through your accommodation the evening before. The mist clears about an hour after sunrise, so plan to set out around
Buy T'nalak from a workshop or an authorized shop. Machine-made imitations exist, so confirm you're getting a genuine handwoven piece.
Always ask permission before photographing T'boli residents. A small donation after a performance or workshop visit is customary.
It's chilly at dawn and at night on the highland. Bring a thin long-sleeve shirt and a windbreaker.

The seven falls, weaving workshops, museums, and viewpoints are spread apart, so the convenient way to see them is to charter a habal-habal driver for half a day or a full day. Rather than haggling every time you get on, it's better to agree on where you'll stop and the total fare before you set off.
A magnitude 7.8 earthquake off Sarangani on
June 8, 2026
collapsed houses and badly damaged roads, bridges, and schools in Lake Sebu and neighboring Tboli, and Lake Sebu declared a state of calamity on
June 17

. Recovery is ongoing, with some sections of the Tboli–General Santos road collapsed and closed and neighboring Lake Holon closed to visits because of landslides, so before you leave, check with the tourism office or your accommodation whether the seven falls, ziplines, and lodgings are open and what the road conditions are on the way. Aftershocks may continue, so also check your accommodation's evacuation instructions.

Travel advisories are in effect for South Cotabato and parts of surrounding Mindanao. Check your home country's latest travel advisory before you go, avoid traveling at night, and stick to main roads and tourist areas.
Letting the local tourism office or your accommodation know your arrival and itinerary makes it easier to get help in an emergency. If traveling alone, it's best to go with a trusted local guide.
The zipline has weight and health restrictions. Avoid it if you have high blood pressure, heart disease, or a back injury.
During the wet season, mountain trails and rocks around the falls get very slippery, and the current in the waterfall pools can suddenly strengthen. It's safer to swim only where it's permitted.
T'nalak patterns and traditional T'boli dress carry sacred meaning for the community. Avoid trying them on casually or taking mocking photos.
The mountain road to Lake Sebu has almost no streetlights after dark. Finish your travel during daylight hours, and avoid setting out on a long journey after
4 p.m.
